name: Dzongkha
notes:
Dzongkha (རྫོང་ཁ), national language of Bhutan, written in the Tibetan script (Uchen/Joyi). The spec resolves the Tibetan SYLLABLE, not the letter: Tibetan spelling is historical, and a syllable is prefix + superscript + ROOT + subjoined + vowel + suffix + post-suffix, of which only the root, the vowel and some suffixes are pronounced (van Driem 1998 ch. 2-3).

How each part is expressed:
* STACKS are grapheme keys. A superscribed or subjoined letter is a combining mark (U+0F90..U+0FBC), so ⟨སྤྲ⟩, ⟨ཁྱ⟩, ⟨ཀྲ⟩, ⟨ལྷ⟩ are single orthographic clusters and map to single onsets — ⟨ཁྱ⟩ = /t͡ɕʰ/, ⟨ཁྲ⟩ = /ʈʰ/, ⟨ལྷ⟩ = /ɬ/. ⟨གཡ⟩ and ⟨དབ⟩ are the two fixed digraphs of the same kind written with full letters.
* PREFIXED letters ⟨ག ད བ མ འ⟩ are silent: positional_graphemes silences them before a consonant. Being silent they carry no inherent vowel either.
* The TSHEG ⟨་⟩ is a mapped grapheme with an empty realisation. It is the syllable delimiter, and mapping it keeps every positional and allophonic context syllable-local instead of letting a suffix rule reach across a syllable boundary.
* SUFFIXES ⟨ས ད ལ ར⟩ are not realised after a nucleus; they umlaut and lengthen it instead (⟨ཁྱོད⟩ [t͡ɕʰøː], ⟨གཉིས⟩ [ɲiː]), and the post-suffix ⟨ས⟩ is never pronounced. ⟨ག ང ན མ བ⟩ stay as codas.
* A BOUND final syllable — ⟨པ⟩/⟨མ⟩/⟨ཝ⟩ written with no tsheg before it — loses its vowel and closes the syllable in front of it (⟨རྒྱལཔོ⟩ [t͡ɕɛːp]); only the vowel loss is stated here, because the engine's rule layer cannot see that the bound consonant itself is a coda and not a fresh onset.
* TONE is a two-way register contrast, and it is derivable from the spelling: the ROOT letter's historical voicing decides it — voiceless root = high ˥, voiced root = low ˩ (Mazaudon & Michailovsky 1988). A sonorant root under a superscript or a prefix is voiceless and takes the high register. The register is written on the syllable nucleus, which is where the WikiPron gold marks it.

Voicing: ⟨ག ད བ ཛ⟩ are the historically 'voiced' letters and are phonetically PLAIN (unaspirated) stops in Standard Dzongkha, contrasting with ⟨ཀ/ཁ⟩, ⟨ཏ/ཐ⟩, ⟨པ/ཕ⟩, ⟨ཙ/ཚ⟩ by aspiration and by register, not by voicing; the fricatives ⟨ཞ ཟ⟩ keep their voicing (/ʑ z/, van Driem 1998 §2.2).

KNOWN CEILING. A Tibetan syllable of exactly two letters and no written vowel sign is structurally ambiguous: ⟨དང⟩ is root+suffix [tɑŋ] while ⟨དངོས⟩ is prefix+root. Telling them apart needs a syllable parser that reads the whole syllable before choosing, which this engine's left-to-right positional resolution cannot do, so the prefix reading is taken uniformly and the root+suffix spellings are read wrong. That, gold rows transcribed narrowly (⟨ཉི་མ⟩ [njimɑ] for /ɲimɑ/), and lexicalised readings are what is left of the residual PER — see docs/benchmarks.md.

Classical Tibetan liturgical/literary adstrate: Dzongkha spelling is conservative and reflects the Classical Tibetan written stack system.
